output.impression: PHES -7, abnormal across all five subtests, reflecting slowed psychomotor speed and impaired attention. The battery is validated for covert hepatic encephalopathy and was administered during an acute encephalopathy and sedative medication effect, so the score describes current impairment and cannot by itself establish a covert baseline.
recommended_actions: Repeat testing after recovery from the acute encephalopathy

alternatives: Melatonin or non-pharmacological measures for insomnia
Non-sedating treatment of anxiety at doses adjusted for hepatic impairment, after recovery
contraindications: Abrupt discontinuation of long-term clonazepam: risk of withdrawal seizures
Flumazenil in long-term benzodiazepine use: can precipitate acute withdrawal and seizures
interactions: Clonazepam in cirrhosis: cleared by hepatic CYP3A4 oxidation; clearance falls and the half-life lengthens in cirrhosis, so a dose increase accumulates over several weeks and prolongs CNS depression
Clonazepam with quetiapine: additive CNS depression; quetiapine is also extensively metabolised by the liver (CYP3A4) and its clearance is reduced in hepatic impairment
Spironolactone with lactulose: lactulose-induced diarrhoea can cause volume depletion and electrolyte disturbance; monitor sodium, potassium and creatinine
Lactulose and rifaximin: no clinically relevant interaction with clonazepam, quetiapine or spironolactone
output.proposed: Clonazepam 1 mg twice daily and quetiapine 25 mg nightly in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy; spironolactone 50 mg daily; lactulose to be started
warnings: Avoid other sedative drugs (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, sedating antihistamines, opioids) in hepatic encephalopathy
If a benzodiazepine is unavoidable during withdrawal, lorazepam or oxazepam (glucuronidated, no active metabolites) accumulate less than clonazepam in cirrhosis

action_criteria.label: Medication review of clonazepam and quetiapine in cirrhosis, with spironolactone, lactulose and rifaximin
action_criteria.rationale: Sedative accumulation precipitated this episode, so the clonazepam reduction and taper, stopping quetiapine and avoiding other sedatives change management [ACG_HE_2026]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.
Do not stop long-term clonazepam abruptly, and do not give flumazenil to reverse it: both risk withdrawal seizures.
Do not dismiss hepatic encephalopathy because the ammonia is only mildly raised, and do not grade it by the ammonia level.
Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor for the prior MCI label before HE and sedative toxicity have been treated and cognition reassessed.
required_recommendations: Identify and treat the precipitant: clonazepam accumulation (84 ng/mL after a dose increase) with quetiapine. Reduce clonazepam to his previous 0.5 mg nightly dose, holding doses while he is drowsy because the accumulated drug clears over days, then taper it off over 2-4 weeks under supervision rather than stopping abruptly (withdrawal seizure risk); stop quetiapine and do not substitute another sedative.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.

Start lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day, taper clonazepam under supervision, and review adherence and symptoms at 4-8 weeks; failure to improve with adherence should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis (ACG 2026 key concept 8).

Once the overt episode has resolved and the sedatives are withdrawn, reassess cognition with psychometric testing (PHES) for covert HE and revise the prior mild cognitive impairment diagnosis accordingly.

Re-evaluate the 'cryptogenic' cirrhosis etiology: PEth or CDT for alcohol, hepatitis B and C serology, autoimmune markers (AMA, ANA, ASMA), ferritin and transferrin saturation, ceruloplasmin, and metabolic risk factors.
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE and diuretic-treated ascites, MELD-Na 13 (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
FDG PET has no role in HE workup; metabolic encephalopathy is reversible with precipitant control and does not require nuclear functional imaging.

accepted: Overt hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), cryptogenic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 13), precipitated by clonazepam accumulation in liver disease after a dose increase (serum level 84 ng/mL, supratherapeutic) plus quetiapine CNS depression; the prior 'MCI' diagnosis may have been unrecognised covert HE.

differential.diagnosis: Benzodiazepine (clonazepam) accumulation / toxicity as sole cause
differential.key_features: Serum clonazepam 84 ng/mL after a dose increase in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis, with frontal beta activity on EEG; it explains much of the sedation, but asterixis, liver dysfunction and diffuse theta slowing indicate HE as well, so the accumulation is the precipitant rather than the whole explanation.
Quetiapine 25 mg is low dose; contributes mildly via CNS depression.
Age 47 with a subacute 3-week decline, asterixis and diffuse EEG slowing in cirrhosis favour HE with sedative toxicity; diffuse atrophy on CT is non-specific; cognition is reassessed after recovery.
Serum ethanol below 10 mg/dL and no withdrawal signs; possible past heavy use bears on the 'cryptogenic' cirrhosis etiology (PEth, CDT), not on this encephalopathy.
No magnetic gait / incontinence triad; CT shows atrophy not ventriculomegaly.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status.

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Covert HE is minimal HE or West Haven grade 1; overt HE is grade 2 or higher (ACG 2026 key concept 1). Lethargy, disorientation to time and asterixis make this episode grade 2, overt.
Child-Pugh B (7: bilirubin 1.6 1, albumin 3.0 2, INR 1.4 1, no ascites on examination while on spironolactone 1, HE grade 2 2); MELD-Na 13 (creatinine 0.9, bilirubin 1.6, INR 1.4, sodium 136)

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.

A prior 'MCI' label in a patient with cirrhosis should be re-examined for covert HE with psychometric testing once any overt episode has resolved and sedatives are withdrawn; the treatment differs (lactulose rather than cholinesterase inhibitors).
Benzodiazepines cleared by hepatic oxidation, such as clonazepam, accumulate in cirrhosis; a dose increase can reach toxic levels over several weeks.

When the diagnosis is uncertain, the theragnostic approach reviews adherence and symptoms after 4-8 weeks of lactulose; failure to improve with adherence should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis (ACG 2026 key concept 8).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: MCI at age 46 in a patient with cirrhosis is atypical for neurodegeneration; covert HE is more likely and is tested with psychometrics once the overt episode has resolved.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Expected from prescribed clonazepam; the supratherapeutic serum level confirms accumulation, but asterixis, liver dysfunction and diffuse theta slowing show that HE is also present: the accumulation is the precipitant, not an alternative explanation.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Assume the cause is straightforward 'benzo accumulation' and miss the concurrent hepatic encephalopathy.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. E. is a 47-year-old man with Child-Pugh B cirrhosis (etiology 'cryptogenic'; family denies alcohol use) and a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment made 1 year ago during hepatology follow-up, now presenting with a 3-week history of worsening confusion and personality change. His sister brought him in after he was found wandering his apartment unable to remember what day it was or where he put things. The timeline is insidious: she notes gradual worsening over weeks rather than acute change. Five weeks ago his primary care physician increased his clonazepam from 0.5 mg nightly to 1 mg twice daily for worsening anxiety; he also takes quetiapine 25 mg nightly for insomnia. He has no jaundice, no ascites on exam, and no fetor hepaticus.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Lethargic, opens eyes to voice. GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Disoriented to time (day, date and month); oriented to place and person. Slow processing. No asterixis on first exam. Mild asterixis detected on repeat exam 4 hours later. Repeating questions. Agitated when redirected. Prior diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment makes baseline unclear.
